summary:
The legal framework a trans visitor meets in Colombia is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. The official Reyes, who defended the change, described those examinations as "profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice".

Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition, without a surgical requirement. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015, and national identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025. A comprehensive trans law was still under legislative consideration in 2025.

The courts have also intervened directly in detention. A Colombian court ruled on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty, protecting the rights of trans detainees in the prison system.

The gap between that framework and enforcement is severe. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders in Colombia between January and May 2025 alone. The UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, completed a fact-finding mission across several Colombian cities in May 2025, praising the government's legal reforms and commitment to equality while warning that institutional progress and daily lived experience are disconnected, and that widespread discrimination and violence against LGBT people must be addressed urgently as killings rise.

The sharpest risk sits where armed groups operate, including in territories under their control. In the department of Caquetá, armed groups ran "social cleansing" campaigns announced through flyer campaigns targeting "drug addicts, prostitutes and faggots", and threatened a further wave. Trans women in that department reported few options beyond sex work; Tatiana Cespedes, a trans salon owner, was forced to relocate twice after receiving death threats from armed men, and a friend of the trans woman Yesenia Rodríguez was killed. In the department of Guajira, armed groups posted flyers from March 2024 carrying a kill list of named individuals under the wording "All will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans".

Targeted killings of trans people continue in the country's ordinary, urban settings. Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was attacked in Bello, Antioquia, near Medellín in April 2025. A 28-second video of the assault went viral from 5 April, showing her with fractured legs, arms and hands, flailing in a creek unable to swim, before she drowned; her mother Sandra Borja stated, "They killed her for being who she was". President Petro ordered an urgent investigation, and solidarity events were held in several cities. One report counted 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025.

Some of this violence has been prosecuted as an international crime rather than ordinary homicide. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, with the state acknowledging that conflict-driven violence against these individuals constitutes gender persecution, a crime against humanity. The UN Human Rights Committee has registered concern over the same pattern.
tangentialFactors:
Colombia's situation is distinctive for how much of the protection it extends comes from the judiciary and transitional justice rather than from the statute book alone. The 2015 notary-based marker change, the 1993 Constitutional Court recognition doctrine, and the 2023 Special Jurisdiction for Peace indictment are all products of courts and peace-process bodies, and the Attorney General's Office is the institution recording LGBTI homicides while the courts recognise gender persecution.

The President Petro government has positioned itself as aligned with LGBTIQ+ equality, which is why the UN Independent Expert Reid found the reforms themselves credible even as he documented the violence. The political direction and the security outcome point in opposite directions, and the mismatch is documented by UN bodies rather than asserted by advocacy groups.

Colombia's decades-long armed conflict is the structural context for the most severe documented risks. Kill-lists and "social cleansing" campaigns are attributed to armed groups, not to private individuals acting alone, and they intersect with the country's history of persecution of people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities in the context of conflict.

Within Latin America the country pairs one of the region's broadest document and family-law regimes with homicide figures of a scale that most other regional jurisdictions with comparable legal recognition do not report.
localsOnly:
Trans Colombians change the sex marker on national identification documents by signing a document before a notary, without physical examinations or psychiatric assessments. The notary procedure replaced a judicial route under which judges ordered invasive examinations.

Legal gender recognition rests on self-recognition under Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993, with no surgical requirement. Identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025. A comprehensive trans law remained under legislative consideration in 2025, so some trans-specific entitlements still depend on court rulings rather than on a consolidated statute.

Same-sex marriage has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015.

A Colombian court has ruled on the treatment of trans women deprived of liberty, protecting the rights of trans detainees and addressing how the prison system must handle trans prisoners.

Residents of armed-group-controlled territories, including in Caquetá and Guajira, report flyer campaigns listing named LGBTQ people for violence, with trans women in those departments facing forced relocation and limited livelihood options beyond sex work. Trans women working in public-facing businesses have been driven out by armed men issuing death threats.

The Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, with the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution, which opens a formal channel for victims in the armed-conflict setting.
outOfScopeNotes:
The status of the comprehensive trans law legislated in 2025 is unresolved in the source inventory: it is reported as being under consideration, but no source confirms enactment, its scope, or whether it is in force at the time of publication.

Full-year 2025 homicide totals for trans and LGBTI people are not sourced. Available figures are partial and differently defined, so they are not directly comparable: the Attorney General's Office counted 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025, while a separate report counted 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025, and a 2024 report counted more than 40 transgender women killed in 2023.

No source in the inventory addresses entry or visa rules for trans visitors, the treatment of foreign trans documents at Colombian border and airport controls, whether screeners or officials may question a traveller's gender presentation, or whether the domestic notary-based marker procedure is available to non-residents or visitors.

Healthcare, asylum and hate-crime sentencing provisions for trans people are not sourced here. There is no inventory item on whether Colombia maintains trans-specific hate-crime aggravation in the criminal code, and none on access to gender-affirming care, insurance coverage, or waiting lists.

Facilities, such as access to gendered bathrooms, changing rooms and shelters on the basis of identity documents, are not covered by the inventory, and neither are detention conditions beyond the single court ruling on trans detainees, which is reported without its case number, date or court name.

Whether the notary-based ID change procedure operates consistently across the national territory is unresolved; the sources describe the rule change and its rationale but contain no implementation data.
